questions.stem: A team has 5 Lambda functions that all depend on the same NumPy/Pandas binary stack (~150MB). They want to share that dependency without duplicating it inside every deployment package. Which fits?

options.text: Package the dependencies into a Lambda layer and attach the layer to each function.
Bundle them into every Lambda zip individually.
Store them in S3 and download at cold start.
Run all 5 functions inside a single Lambda.

questions.explanation: Lambda layers exist exactly to share runtime dependencies across functions. Packaging in each zip duplicates storage and slows cold starts; S3 download adds latency.

questions.stem: A user-facing Lambda has occasional cold-start latency spikes that hurt UX. Latency budget is < 200ms 99th percentile. Which fits BEST?

options.text: Configure provisioned concurrency on the function (or alias) at the expected baseline.
Increase the Lambda memory to 10GB and hope.
Add SnapStart for Python (Java/Snap only — not applicable here).
Disable the function during off-hours.

questions.explanation: Provisioned concurrency keeps a configured number of execution environments warm. Memory tweaks help CPU but not init time. SnapStart applies to Java/.NET/Python (with limits — but the question implies Lambda generally; the canonical answer for cold starts is provisioned concurrency).

questions.stem: A REST API needs request transformation and per-stage URL `/v1/...` `/v2/...` with request/response mapping templates. Which API Gateway type fits?

options.text: REST API (with method/integration request/response mappings + stages).
HTTP API only — has no transformations.
WebSocket API.
A direct ALB.

questions.explanation: REST APIs support full mapping templates and stages. HTTP APIs are leaner/cheaper but don't support mapping-template transformations. WebSocket is for bidirectional. ALB doesn't have API-stage transformations.

questions.stem: A workflow has < 5-minute, very high-throughput execution and per-execution cost matters more than fully audited history. Which Step Functions workflow type fits?

options.text: Express workflow.
Standard workflow.
A single Lambda doing everything.
A cron-based EC2.

questions.explanation: Express is optimized for high-throughput, short-duration workflows and bills per execution + ms. Standard supports up to 1 year, full history, exactly-once. Lambda alone misses orchestration semantics.

questions.stem: A DynamoDB table needs an additional access pattern: queries by `customerId + createdAt` while the base table keys on `orderId`. Which fits?

options.text: Create a Global Secondary Index (GSI) with `customerId` as PK and `createdAt` as SK.
Run a Scan with filter for every customer.
Add a Local Secondary Index — but LSI only works when the partition key is the SAME as the base table's.
Migrate to RDS.

questions.explanation: GSIs enable arbitrary alternate access patterns — different PK from base. LSIs require the same PK as the base table. Scans are expensive and slow. Migration is unnecessary.

questions.stem: Two writers must update an item only if the current `version` attribute matches what they read (optimistic concurrency). Which DynamoDB feature fits?

options.text: A conditional write using a `ConditionExpression` on the `version` attribute.
A Scan + delete pattern.
A separate "lock" item using putItem with overwrite.
Stop one of the writers.

questions.explanation: Conditional writes are DynamoDB's native optimistic-concurrency primitive. The other options are wrong shape or anti-patterns.

questions.stem: Whenever an item is modified in a DynamoDB table, a downstream service must reliably react with at-least-once semantics. Which feature fits?

options.text: Enable DynamoDB Streams and consume via Lambda (or Kinesis adapter).
Poll the table every second with Scan.
Trigger CloudFront invalidation.
Use SES.

questions.explanation: DynamoDB Streams emit ordered change records consumable by Lambda (event-source mapping). Polling with Scan is expensive and unreliable.

questions.stem: A producer publishes one message per order. Consumers Email, Inventory, and Analytics each must receive every order. Which fits?

options.text: SNS topic with three SQS subscriptions (one queue per consumer) — fan-out pattern.
A single SQS queue shared by all three (each message would be delivered to only one consumer).
CloudWatch alarms.
A Lambda calling each consumer synchronously.

questions.explanation: SNS → multiple SQS subscriptions is the canonical fan-out pattern with isolation per consumer. A shared SQS only delivers each message once. Synchronous chains tightly couple producer to all consumers.

questions.stem: You need exactly-once message processing with strict ordering by `customerId` for an order pipeline. Which fits?

options.text: SQS FIFO queue with `MessageGroupId = customerId` and content-based deduplication.
SQS Standard queue.
SNS Standard topic.
Kinesis Data Firehose with no shard key.

questions.explanation: SQS FIFO with MessageGroupId provides exactly-once + per-group FIFO ordering. Standard queues are at-least-once with best-effort ordering.

questions.stem: A Lambda must run on a cron schedule every weekday at 09:00 UTC. Which is the cleanest trigger?

options.text: An EventBridge schedule (or rule) with cron expression invoking the Lambda.
A 24/7 EC2 instance running a cron daemon that invokes the Lambda.
A spinning Lambda that sleeps until 09:00.
A user clicking a button.

questions.explanation: EventBridge Scheduler / scheduled rules with cron expressions are the canonical AWS scheduled trigger. The other options are wasteful, fragile, or absurd.

questions.stem: Which TWO are valid ways to integrate API Gateway with backend logic?

options.text: Lambda proxy integration (request/response passed transparently to/from Lambda).
AWS service integration (API Gateway calls another AWS service such as DynamoDB or SQS directly).
Hard-coded responses inside CloudFront only.
Embedded SQL in the API Gateway URL itself.
A 3rd-party UDP socket.

questions.explanation: Lambda proxy and AWS service integrations are documented API Gateway integration types. The other options are not valid integration patterns.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about uploading large files to S3 are TRUE?

options.text: Multipart upload allows resumable parallel uploads of objects larger than 5GB (and is recommended for objects >100MB).
Presigned URLs let a client upload directly to S3 without proxying through your backend.
S3 has a hard maximum object size of 5MB.
Single PUT supports objects up to 5TB.
Presigned URLs require the client to know your IAM access keys.

questions.explanation: Multipart and presigned URLs are correct. S3 single PUT is capped at 5GB (not 5TB and not 5MB). Presigned URLs do NOT expose keys to the client.

questions.stem: A web/mobile app needs end-user sign-up and sign-in (email + password, social IdPs) with managed user directory and tokens. Which Cognito feature fits?

options.text: Cognito User Pools.
Cognito Identity Pools (federated identities) only — those exchange tokens for AWS creds, not user directory.
IAM users — one per app user.
AWS Directory Service.

questions.explanation: User Pools = end-user directory + sign-in/up + tokens. Identity Pools complement them by exchanging tokens for temporary AWS credentials. IAM users for app end-users is an anti-pattern.

questions.stem: A signed-in app user must call AWS APIs (e.g., upload to S3) directly from the browser with TEMPORARY credentials scoped to their identity. Which fits?

options.text: Cognito Identity Pool — exchange the user pool ID token for temp AWS credentials via STS.
Embed your IAM user access keys in JavaScript.
Use root credentials.
A long-lived Lambda function URL.

questions.explanation: Identity Pools (federated identities) issue short-lived AWS credentials via STS in exchange for a JWT. The other options are critical anti-patterns.

questions.stem: A Lambda needs to read a database password at cold start. The team wants automatic rotation and IAM-controlled access. Which fits?

options.text: Store the password in AWS Secrets Manager and grant the Lambda execution role `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue`.
Hard-code in the deployment package.
Plaintext environment variable named `PASSWORD`.
A public S3 file.

questions.explanation: Secrets Manager supports rotation natively for RDS and IAM-scoped fetching. The other options leak credentials.

questions.stem: A team needs to store NON-secret application config (feature flags, endpoint URLs, sizes) accessible by Lambda — at the lowest cost.

options.text: AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store (Standard tier, free up to 10,000 params).
AWS Secrets Manager (paid per secret per month).
Hard-coded constants requiring redeploy on change.
A public S3 file.

questions.explanation: Parameter Store standard tier is free for non-secret config and integrates with IAM. Secrets Manager is paid and overkill for non-secrets. Constants force redeploys.

questions.stem: A Lambda must encrypt sensitive payloads using a customer-managed KMS key BEFORE storing them in DynamoDB. Which API call should the function use?

options.text: `kms:GenerateDataKey` to get a per-payload data key, then envelope-encrypt the payload locally and store the ciphertext + encrypted-data-key.
Send the plaintext to KMS for encryption every time (works but expensive and capped at 4KB).
Just store plaintext.
Use an SSH tunnel.

questions.explanation: Envelope encryption with GenerateDataKey is the documented pattern for client-side / app-level encryption with KMS. Direct kms:Encrypt has a 4KB plaintext limit and high cost for large payloads.

questions.stem: A Lambda must call DynamoDB. What's the LEAST-privilege way to grant access?

options.text: Attach an IAM policy to the function's execution role granting only the specific DynamoDB actions on the specific table ARN.
Attach `AdministratorAccess` to the role for "simplicity".
Use root credentials inside the Lambda.
Make the table public.

questions.explanation: Least privilege via narrowly scoped role policy on the specific table ARN is the canonical pattern. The other options violate security baselines.

questions.stem: A REST API in API Gateway must be invokable only by IAM-authenticated users in the same account. Which authorizer fits?

options.text: IAM (AWS_IAM) authorization — sign requests with SigV4.
No authorization — public endpoint.
A custom Lambda authorizer that returns "Allow" unconditionally.
Basic Auth in a query string.

questions.explanation: AWS_IAM authorization requires SigV4-signed requests and integrates natively with IAM identity policies. The other options are insecure.

questions.stem: Which TWO are recommended ways to share secrets with an EC2 application?

options.text: Store the secret in AWS Secrets Manager; the app reads it via the instance role.
Store as SecureString in SSM Parameter Store; the app reads it via the instance role.
Bake the secret into the AMI.
Email the secret to every developer.
Hard-code in user-data.

questions.explanation: Secrets Manager and SSM Parameter Store SecureString are the documented secret-distribution patterns. Baking secrets into AMIs / user-data / email is a leak risk.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about API Gateway authorization are TRUE?

options.text: Cognito User Pool authorizers validate JWTs issued by the user pool.
Lambda authorizers (custom) let you implement arbitrary auth logic and return an IAM policy.
API keys alone provide strong authentication (they don't — they're for usage plans/throttling, not auth).
WebSocket APIs cannot use any authorizer.
IAM authorization is impossible for HTTP APIs.

questions.explanation: Cognito and Lambda authorizers are documented API Gateway auth options. API keys are NOT authentication. WebSocket APIs DO support authorizers. HTTP APIs DO support IAM auth.

questions.stem: A team wants minimum-effort blue/green deployments for a Lambda function with automatic CloudWatch-alarm-based rollback. Which fits?

options.text: AWS CodeDeploy with a `Linear10PercentEvery1Minute` (or canary) deployment configuration on the Lambda alias.
Manual `aws lambda update-function-code` and pray.
Re-create the function with a new name on each release.
Disable monitoring during deploys.

questions.explanation: CodeDeploy for Lambda shifts traffic via aliases with linear/canary configs and auto-rolls-back on alarm. The other options are manual / unsafe.

questions.stem: You want to define a serverless app (Lambda + API Gateway + DynamoDB) declaratively with shorter syntax than raw CloudFormation. Which fits?

options.text: AWS SAM (Serverless Application Model) — transforms to CloudFormation under the hood.
Click everything in the console and screenshot for documentation.
A bash script of `aws cli` calls.
Manual API calls from Postman.

questions.explanation: SAM is the AWS-native shorter syntax for serverless on top of CloudFormation. The other options are non-IaC and brittle.

questions.stem: An Elastic Beanstalk web app is deployed with the `Rolling` policy. The team wants an option that keeps capacity at 100% during deploy and rolls back faster on failure. Which fits?

options.text: Immutable deployments — launches a new ASG, only swaps in if healthy; failure has no impact on existing fleet.
AllAtOnce — fastest but full-outage on failure.
Rolling with additional batch — temporarily increases capacity; partial impact on failure.
Rolling — same as the current policy.

questions.explanation: Immutable deploys keep full capacity, run on a fresh ASG, and discard on failure with no impact on running fleet. Rolling/AllAtOnce/Rolling-with-additional-batch trade off differently.

questions.stem: A CI/CD pipeline using CodePipeline runs unit tests, builds a container, and deploys to ECS. Which service should run the build and test stages?

options.text: AWS CodeBuild — fully managed build service, integrates with CodePipeline.
A 24/7 EC2 with Jenkins.
A Lambda doing the build itself.
CloudFormation StackSets.

questions.explanation: CodeBuild is the AWS-managed build service designed for this. The other options are off-pattern.

questions.stem: A team uses CloudFormation. They want to ensure the template is the source of truth and detect when someone manually edits a resource in the console. Which feature fits?

options.text: CloudFormation drift detection.
CloudWatch alarms.
AWS Trusted Advisor.
IAM Access Analyzer.

questions.explanation: CloudFormation drift detection compares the deployed stack with the template and surfaces diffs. The other tools address different concerns.

questions.stem: A buildspec.yml in CodeBuild has a `secrets-manager` mapping. What does that do?

options.text: Fetches secret values from AWS Secrets Manager and injects them as environment variables for the build.
Encrypts the build artifacts at rest.
Hides build logs from CloudWatch.
Disables the build cache.

questions.explanation: CodeBuild has native Secrets Manager (and SSM) integration via env-var mappings — keeps secrets out of source. The other options are unrelated.

questions.stem: A SAM template specifies `AutoPublishAlias: live` on a Lambda function. What does this do?

options.text: Publishes a new function version on every deploy and updates an alias `live` to point to it (commonly paired with CodeDeploy traffic-shifting).
Always invokes the previous version.
Disables CloudWatch logging.
Encrypts the function code.

questions.explanation: AutoPublishAlias is the SAM convention for versioned + aliased deploys, prerequisite for CodeDeploy traffic-shifting. The other options are not what it does.

questions.stem: Which TWO are valid CodePipeline source providers?

options.text: AWS CodeCommit.
GitHub or GitHub Enterprise (via the CodeStar connection).
A USB stick on someone's desk.
Email attachments.
A public S3 bucket without versioning enabled (versioning is required).

questions.explanation: CodeCommit and GitHub are documented source providers; S3 is supported but requires versioning. The other options are not source providers.

questions.stem: A microservice request flows through API Gateway → Lambda → DynamoDB → SNS. The team wants per-segment latency and error visualisation. Which service fits?

options.text: AWS X-Ray with the SDK instrumented in Lambda (and active tracing on API Gateway).
A single CloudWatch alarm.
AWS Trusted Advisor.
A custom log file on EC2.

questions.explanation: X-Ray traces requests across AWS services and renders a service map with latency/error breakdown. The other options don't provide cross-service tracing.

questions.stem: A team needs ad-hoc SQL-like analysis of CloudWatch Logs (filter by status code, group by URL, calc P95 latency). Which fits?

options.text: CloudWatch Logs Insights — purpose-built query language over CloudWatch Logs.
Download all logs and grep them on a laptop.
Use SES.
CloudFront access logs only.

questions.explanation: CloudWatch Logs Insights is the documented AWS log-analysis tool — purpose-built for ad-hoc queries. The other options are off-pattern.

questions.stem: Lambda invocations from API Gateway return `429` errors at peak. Which is the most likely cause and fix?

options.text: Account- or function-level concurrency limit hit; raise the function's reserved concurrency or request a Service Quotas increase.
API Gateway disabled itself.
CloudFront throttled the requests.
IAM permission missing.

questions.explanation: Lambda 429/TooManyRequestsException is concurrency throttling. The other causes don't produce 429 from Lambda.

questions.stem: An app emits per-request custom CloudWatch metrics from inside Lambda — but bills are spiking. Which optimisation fits BEST?

options.text: Use the Embedded Metric Format (EMF) so metrics are extracted from log lines (1 PutMetricData equivalent for many metrics, lower cost).
Just disable the metrics.
Move every metric to a Slack message.
Use CloudWatch Logs only — no metrics.

questions.explanation: EMF is the documented cost-efficient way to publish high-cardinality custom metrics from logs. The other options either hide problems or aren't equivalent.

questions.stem: A DynamoDB application receives `ProvisionedThroughputExceededException` despite estimated traffic being below allocated capacity. Which is the likely root cause?

options.text: A "hot partition" — uneven access concentrated on one PK; redesign keys for even distribution or use adaptive capacity / on-demand mode.
IAM permission denied.
KMS rotation conflict.
CloudWatch is broken.

questions.explanation: Throughput exceeded with average usage low almost always means a hot partition. Adaptive capacity helps automatically; on-demand or key redesign solves it. The other causes wouldn't produce that exception.

questions.stem: Which TWO improvements REDUCE Lambda cold-start latency?

options.text: Configure provisioned concurrency on a hot alias.
Reduce deployment package size and minimise top-level imports.
Add many unused dependencies "just in case".
Disable VPC config (where possible) — but only if VPC isn't needed; modern Lambda VPC has improved cold start, this is situational.
Run the Lambda in a region thousands of km away from users.

questions.explanation: Provisioned concurrency and lean packages directly reduce cold-start latency. Adding unused deps and routing through far regions worsens it.
